stem: Where was the United Nations Charter signed in June 1945?

options.text: San Francisco
Geneva
New York
Bretton Woods

explanation: Delegates signed the Charter in San Francisco on 26 June 1945. The conference followed wartime planning for a new international organisation.

stem: On what date did the United Nations Charter enter into force?

options.text: 10 December 1948
24 October 1945
26 June 1945
1 January 1942

explanation: The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945 after the required ratifications. The date is observed as United Nations Day.

stem: Which international organisation was created by the Charter signed at the San Francisco Conference?

options.text: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization
The European Economic Community
The United Nations
The League of Nations

explanation: The Charter established the United Nations as an international organisation. The League of Nations was its predecessor, not the body created in San Francisco.

stem: Which wartime conference agreed on a framework for a post-war international organisation before San Francisco?

options.text: Potsdam Conference
Casablanca Conference
Locarno Conference
Dumbarton Oaks Conference

explanation: The Dumbarton Oaks talks in 1944 produced proposals for a new international organisation. The San Francisco Conference later negotiated and adopted the Charter.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders the creation of the United Nations?

options.text: Dumbarton Oaks proposals → San Francisco signing → Charter enters into force
Charter enters into force → Dumbarton Oaks proposals → San Francisco signing
San Francisco signing → Dumbarton Oaks proposals → Charter enters into force
Potsdam Conference → Charter enters into force → Dumbarton Oaks proposals

explanation: Proposals were developed at Dumbarton Oaks in 1944, the Charter was signed in June 1945 and it entered into force in October 1945.

stem: What central purpose is stated in the opening of the UN Charter?

options.text: To administer every former colony directly
To maintain international peace and security
To establish a single world government
To create a common currency for all states

explanation: The Charter identifies the maintenance of international peace and security as a central purpose. It also sets out cooperation and human-rights goals.

stem: Which principle in Article 2 of the UN Charter recognises the sovereign equality of member states?

options.text: All states must use the same constitution
Every member has a permanent Security Council seat
All members are sovereign equals
The Security Council has no special powers

explanation: Article 2 states the principle of sovereign equality among members. It does not give every state identical roles in every UN organ.

stem: What does Article 2(4) of the UN Charter require states to refrain from doing?

options.text: Taking part in General Assembly debates
Trading with states outside their region
Joining a regional organisation
Threatening or using force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence

explanation: Article 2(4) prohibits the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence, subject to Charter provisions.

stem: Which method does the UN Charter encourage for resolving international disputes?

options.text: Peaceful settlement
Unilateral annexation
Permanent economic blockade
Secret military occupation

explanation: The Charter calls on members to settle disputes by peaceful means. The specific method depends on the dispute and the parties involved.

stem: What does the Charter mean by the principle of non-intervention in domestic jurisdiction, subject to enforcement measures?

options.text: States may ignore all treaty obligations
The UN generally should not intervene in matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction
The Security Council cannot address any conflict
The General Assembly cannot discuss international matters

explanation: Article 2(7) limits UN intervention in domestic matters while preserving enforcement action under Chapter VII. It is not a blanket exemption from international obligations.

stem: Which statement best describes the purposes of the United Nations?

options.text: To establish a single global army under the General Assembly
To replace national courts in every legal dispute
To maintain peace, develop friendly relations and promote international cooperation
To dissolve all national governments

explanation: The Charter combines peace and security with cooperation and friendly relations among nations. It does not establish a world government or universal domestic court system.

stem: How many principal organs were established by the original UN Charter?

options.text: Three
Five
Ten
Six

explanation: The Charter established six principal organs. They are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council, International Court of Justice and Secretariat.

stem: Which principal UN organ includes all member states?

options.text: The General Assembly
The Security Council
The International Court of Justice
The Secretariat

explanation: The General Assembly is the UN's plenary organ, with each member state represented. Its powers differ from those of the Security Council.

stem: Which UN organ has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security?

options.text: The International Court of Justice
The Security Council
The Economic and Social Council
The General Assembly Secretariat

explanation: Article 24 gives the Security Council primary responsibility for international peace and security. The Charter assigns distinct functions to the other principal organs.

stem: Which UN organ coordinates work on economic, social and related international issues?

options.text: The International Court of Justice
The Trusteeship Council
The Economic and Social Council
The Security Council

explanation: The Economic and Social Council coordinates work in economic and social fields. It is a principal organ established by the Charter.

stem: What is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations?

options.text: The International Criminal Court
The Permanent Court of Arbitration
The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg
The International Court of Justice

explanation: The International Court of Justice is the UN's principal judicial organ. It hears cases between states and gives advisory opinions when authorised.

stem: Which principal UN organ carries out the organisation's day-to-day administrative work?

options.text: The Secretariat
The Security Council
The General Assembly
The International Court of Justice

explanation: The Secretariat carries out the UN's administrative work under the authority of the Secretary-General. It is one of the six principal organs.

stem: Which principal organ was established to supervise the international trusteeship system?

options.text: The International Court of Justice
The Trusteeship Council
The Economic and Social Council
The Security Council

explanation: The Trusteeship Council supervised trust territories under the Charter system. It suspended operations after the last trust territory became independent.

stem: What is the main role of the UN General Assembly under the Charter?

options.text: To issue binding judgments in cases between states
To appoint every national government
To discuss matters within the Charter's scope and make recommendations
To command all national armed forces

explanation: The General Assembly may discuss Charter matters and make recommendations, subject to Charter limits. It does not operate as a world parliament with direct authority over national governments.

stem: Which group of states were named as permanent members of the Security Council in the original Charter?

options.text: China, India, France, the United Kingdom and the United States
Germany, Japan, Italy, the Soviet Union and the United States
France, Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States
China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States

explanation: Article 23 named China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States as permanent members. This is the original Charter wording for the post-war body.

stem: What is the veto in the UN Security Council?

options.text: A negative vote by a permanent member that blocks a substantive decision
A vote by any General Assembly member to reject a treaty
A judicial appeal to the International Court of Justice
A procedural motion to delay a Secretariat report

explanation: On substantive matters, a negative vote by a permanent member prevents adoption of a draft resolution. Procedural decisions are treated differently under Article 27.

stem: Which type of Security Council decision is not subject to the permanent-member veto under Article 27?

options.text: A decision admitting a new member after recommendation
A procedural decision
A decision authorising enforcement action
A decision imposing sanctions

explanation: Article 27 distinguishes procedural decisions from other matters that require the concurring votes of permanent members. The veto applies to substantive decisions, not procedural votes.

stem: What responsibility does Article 24 assign to the Security Council?

options.text: International monetary cooperation
Judicial review of national legislation
Primary responsibility for international peace and security
Administration of the UN Secretariat

explanation: Article 24 gives the Security Council primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. Members agree that it acts on their behalf in carrying out that role.

stem: How many members did the Security Council have under the original 1945 Charter?

options.text: Five
Fifteen
Twenty-one
Eleven

explanation: The original Charter provided for an eleven-member Security Council: five permanent members and six elected members. The Council was later enlarged to fifteen members in 1965.

stem: Which statement best explains the Security Council veto?

options.text: It gives each permanent member a blocking vote on substantive decisions
It allows any member state to cancel a General Assembly resolution
It enables the Secretary-General to overturn court judgments
It prevents all procedural votes from being adopted

explanation: The veto is a special voting power of the permanent members on substantive questions. It does not apply in the same way to procedural matters.

stem: Which body may recommend a new state's admission to the United Nations before the General Assembly decides?

options.text: The Secretariat alone
The Security Council
The International Court of Justice
The Trusteeship Council

explanation: Under Article 4, admission is decided by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council. Both steps are required.

stem: At which 1944 conference were the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development designed?

options.text: Yalta Conference
Potsdam Conference
Bretton Woods Conference
San Francisco Conference

explanation: Delegates met at Bretton Woods in July 1944 and formulated the agreements for the IMF and IBRD. Both institutions are commonly called Bretton Woods institutions.

stem: Which institution was created to support international monetary cooperation and address balance-of-payments problems?

options.text: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
The International Court of Justice
The United Nations Trusteeship Council
The International Monetary Fund

explanation: The IMF was designed to promote monetary cooperation and provide financial support for balance-of-payments needs. The World Bank has a different development and reconstruction focus.

stem: What was the institution now called the World Bank originally named?

options.text: International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
International Monetary Fund
International Development Association
International Finance Corporation

explanation: The World Bank began with the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development. Its original role included financing reconstruction and development.

stem: Which post-war institution was primarily assigned financing for reconstruction and economic development?

options.text: The International Court of Justice
The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development
The International Monetary Fund
The General Assembly

explanation: The IBRD was assigned a role in reconstruction and development finance. The IMF focused more directly on monetary cooperation and financial stability.

stem: Which agreement emerged from the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944?

options.text: The North Atlantic Treaty
The Treaty of Rome
Articles of Agreement for the IMF and IBRD
The Charter of the United Nations

explanation: The Bretton Woods Conference formulated the Articles of Agreement for the IMF and IBRD. The UN Charter was negotiated later at San Francisco.

stem: Which comparison between the IMF and the World Bank is most accurate?

options.text: The IMF conducts war-crimes trials, while the World Bank supervises the Security Council
The IMF administers trust territories, while the World Bank elects judges
Both institutions are principal organs of the United Nations
The IMF focuses on monetary stability, while the World Bank finances reconstruction and development

explanation: The institutions share a post-war economic framework but have distinct roles. The IMF focuses on monetary cooperation, while the IBRD supports reconstruction and development.

stem: Which agreement established the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg?

options.text: The London Agreement of 8 August 1945
The UN Charter of 26 June 1945
The Treaty of Versailles of 1919
The Geneva Declaration of 1954

explanation: The London Agreement established the International Military Tribunal and included its Charter. The trials addressed senior Nazi leaders after the war.

stem: Which category of crime was explicitly included in the Nuremberg Tribunal's jurisdiction?

options.text: Unlawful trade tariffs
Crimes against humanity
Piracy on the high seas
Tax evasion

explanation: The Tribunal's Charter included crimes against humanity, alongside crimes against peace and war crimes. The category became important in post-war international law.

stem: When did the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg deliver its judgment?

options.text: 26 June 1945
2 September 1945
1 October 1946
8 August 1945

explanation: The Nuremberg Tribunal delivered its judgment on 1 October 1946. The proceedings had begun in November 1945.

stem: Which tribunal tried leading Japanese wartime officials in Tokyo after the war?

options.text: The International Court of Justice
The Nuremberg Military Tribunal
The Permanent Court of Arbitration
The International Military Tribunal for the Far East

explanation: The International Military Tribunal for the Far East held the Tokyo war-crimes trials. It was distinct from the Nuremberg tribunal in Europe.

stem: When did the Tokyo war-crimes tribunal begin its proceedings?

options.text: 1 October 1946
8 August 1945
24 October 1945

explanation: The Tokyo tribunal began on 3 May 1946 and delivered its judgment in November 1948. Its proceedings concerned Japanese wartime leaders.

stem: Which statement best compares the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals?

options.text: They were UN organs created by the Charter's Article 23
They were separate post-war tribunals addressing leaders of defeated Germany and Japan
They were branches of the International Court of Justice established before the war
They tried only military prisoners from the First World War

explanation: Nuremberg and Tokyo were separate post-war tribunals for leaders of Germany and Japan. Neither was a principal organ of the United Nations.

stem: Which Allied powers initially occupied Germany after its defeat in 1945?

options.text: Britain, Italy, Spain and France
France, Poland, China and the Netherlands
The United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union
The United States, China, Italy and Japan

explanation: Germany was occupied by the four principal Allied powers after its surrender. Each administered an occupation zone under the post-war arrangements.

stem: How was Berlin administered immediately after the Second World War?

options.text: It became the capital of a unified neutral Germany
It was governed solely by the United Nations
It was annexed by the Soviet Union
It was divided into sectors administered by the four occupying powers

explanation: Berlin was located within the Soviet occupation zone but was itself divided into sectors administered by the four Allied powers. This arrangement later became a source of conflict.

stem: Which body coordinated the four-power administration of Germany after the war?

options.text: The Allied Control Council
The Security Council
The International Court of Justice
The Bretton Woods Commission

explanation: The Allied Control Council was intended to coordinate the four powers' administration of Germany. Cooperation between the occupying governments later broke down.

stem: Which two German states were established in 1949 during the post-war division?

options.text: The Federal Republic of Austria and the German Confederation
The Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic
The German Empire and the Weimar Republic
East Germany and the Kingdom of Prussia

explanation: In 1949, the western occupation zones became the Federal Republic of Germany and the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic. The division reflected the growing Cold War split.

stem: Which city was divided into occupation sectors despite lying inside the Soviet zone of Germany?

options.text: Hamburg
Munich
Berlin
Bonn

explanation: Berlin was divided into four sectors under Allied administration even though it lay within the Soviet occupation zone. This special status shaped later crises.

stem: Which outcome best describes the post-war status of Germany before the two states were founded?

options.text: It immediately regained full sovereignty as one state
It was administered by the League of Nations
It was annexed in full by France
It was governed by four occupying powers in separate zones

explanation: After the German surrender, the Allies governed Germany through occupation zones. The two German states were founded in 1949, not immediately in 1945.

stem: Which statement about the United Nations and the IMF is correct?

options.text: The UN was created for broad international cooperation, while the IMF focused on monetary cooperation
Both were created as courts to try war criminals
The IMF is a principal organ of the UN Charter
The UN was created solely to finance European reconstruction

explanation: The United Nations has broad purposes set out in its Charter. The IMF is a separate Bretton Woods institution focused on monetary cooperation.

stem: Which institution hears contentious cases between states as its central judicial role?

options.text: The General Assembly
The International Court of Justice
The International Military Tribunal for the Far East
The IMF

explanation: The ICJ hears legal disputes submitted by states and gives advisory opinions when authorised. It does not try individuals for criminal responsibility.

stem: Which statement distinguishes the International Court of Justice from the Nuremberg Tribunal?

options.text: Both courts tried only states for trade disputes
Nuremberg was the judicial organ of the UN General Assembly
The ICJ is a UN principal organ for state cases; Nuremberg tried individual Nazi leaders
The ICJ is a financial institution; Nuremberg was a UN economic body

explanation: The ICJ is the UN's principal judicial organ and deals primarily with disputes between states. Nuremberg was a separate tribunal that tried individuals for international crimes.

stem: What was the purpose of the UN Trusteeship System?

options.text: To divide Germany into occupation zones
To regulate international exchange rates
To prosecute leaders of the Axis powers
To promote the advancement and movement toward self-government of trust territories

explanation: The Trusteeship System was intended to advance inhabitants and guide trust territories toward self-government or independence. It was a post-war international oversight arrangement.

stem: What change did the Trusteeship Council make in 1994?

options.text: It suspended operations after the last trust territory became independent
It governs all non-self-governing territories
It is the UN's principal judicial organ
It was dissolved before the UN Charter entered into force

explanation: The Trusteeship Council suspended operations in 1994 after Palau became independent.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes a General Assembly recommendation from a Security Council decision?

options.text: The General Assembly has no role under the Charter
The Charter gives the two organs different powers and procedures
Every General Assembly recommendation is automatically a binding court judgment
The Security Council may act only after approval by the IMF

explanation: The Charter gives the General Assembly and Security Council distinct functions. The legal effect of an action depends on the organ and the Charter provision used.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders Bretton Woods and the founding of the United Nations?

options.text: UN Charter signed → Bretton Woods agreements → Charter enters into force
Tokyo tribunal begins → Bretton Woods agreements → Dumbarton Oaks
Bretton Woods agreements → UN Charter signed → Charter enters into force
UN Charter enters into force → Bretton Woods agreements → Charter signed

explanation: The Bretton Woods Conference took place in July 1944. The UN Charter was signed in June 1945 and entered into force in October 1945.

stem: Which sequence correctly orders key post-war institutional events?

options.text: Nuremberg judgment → London Agreement → Tokyo judgment
Tokyo judgment → London Agreement → Nuremberg judgment
UN Charter enters into force → London Agreement → Bretton Woods Conference
London Agreement → Nuremberg judgment → Tokyo judgment

explanation: The London Agreement was signed in August 1945, the Nuremberg judgment followed in October 1946, and the Tokyo judgment came in November 1948.

stem: Which statement best captures the post-war institutional order created in the 1940s?

options.text: It combined a general international organisation with specialised economic bodies and criminal tribunals
It placed all international functions under a single UN court
It replaced national governments with a global administration
It was created entirely before the Second World War

explanation: The post-war order included the United Nations, Bretton Woods institutions and separate war-crimes tribunals. They had different mandates and legal bases.

stem: Which original permanent Security Council member was represented by the Soviet Union in the 1945 Charter?

options.text: The People's Republic of China
The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
The Russian Empire
The German Democratic Republic

explanation: The original Charter named the USSR as a permanent member. That wording records the institution's founding context in 1945.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials from the UN's principal organs?

options.text: They replaced the International Court of Justice
They were committees of the IMF
They were post-war tribunals, not organs listed in Article 7 of the UN Charter
They were two additional Security Council chambers

explanation: The tribunals were created by separate agreements and occupation authorities. Article 7 lists six principal UN organs and does not include them.

stem: Which pairing is correct?

options.text: IMF — war-crimes trials; IBRD — Security Council vetoes
IMF — trusteeship oversight; IBRD — state-to-state court cases
IMF — German occupation; IBRD — UN Charter interpretation
IMF — monetary cooperation; IBRD — reconstruction and development finance

explanation: The IMF and IBRD were created within the Bretton Woods framework but were assigned different roles. The IMF dealt with monetary cooperation and the IBRD with reconstruction and development finance.

stem: Which combination correctly matches a post-war body with its function?

options.text: International Court of Justice — legal disputes between states
Security Council — financing development projects
IMF — deciding territorial cases
Trusteeship Council — prosecuting war criminals

explanation: The ICJ's role is to hear cases between states and provide advisory opinions under its statute. The other bodies listed have different mandates.

stem: Which requirement allowed the UN Charter to enter into force in October 1945?

options.text: A vote by the Bretton Woods institutions
Ratification by the five permanent members and a majority of other signatories
Approval by every country in the world
A judgment from the International Court of Justice

explanation: Article 110 required ratification by the five permanent Security Council members and a majority of the other signatories. The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945.

stem: Which statement about the post-war division of Germany is accurate?

options.text: Berlin was administered only by France
The Security Council created the occupation zones in 1949
Four-power occupation preceded the creation of East and West German states
The two German states were established before Germany surrendered

explanation: The four-power occupation began after Germany's defeat. The Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic were founded later, in 1949.

stem: Which conclusion best explains why the UN, IMF and IBRD should not be treated as interchangeable organisations?

options.text: They all have the same membership and legal powers
They are all principal organs created by Article 7 of the UN Charter
They were all international criminal courts
They were designed for different tasks under separate founding agreements

explanation: The UN Charter and Bretton Woods agreements established organisations with different mandates. Their shared post-war setting does not make their roles interchangeable.
